title: Mongolia's Buddhism
hookLine: Vajrayana among the Mongols, and its return since 1990

lines: AN OLD MAN, A PRAYER WHEEL.
cards: An old man in a long padded coat turns a row of prayer wheels, one after another, at a monastery on a hill in Ulaanbaatar, his breath white in the cold.
Behind him, a line of boys in maroon robes hurries toward the assembly hall, late for chanting. The old man remembers when the halls were silent and the robes were gone. The boys never knew that.
They just know the chanting starts at a certain hour, and they're late. Between his memory and their rush is the story of Mongolia's Buddhism.

teach.h: ALTAN KHAN AND THE OCEAN TITLE.
teach.b: Mongol rulers and Tibetan lamas met more than once in history, and one meeting stands out. A Mongol ruler, Altan Khan, met the Gelug teacher Sonam Gyatso and gave him a title, Dalai: the Mongolian word for ocean.
Tradition says that is where the name Dalai Lama comes from. Mongolia took up Tibetan Buddhism deeply, with its own monasteries, its own scholars writing in Tibetan, and its own tulkus.
One of them, Zanabazar, was a Mongol prince who became a great teacher and also an artist.

His gilded bronze buddhas, calm and graceful, are still treasured in Mongolia. He worked within the same rules as the thangka painters and made something unmistakably Mongolian. Then came the silence.
Under communist rule, religion was crushed.

Monasteries were closed and torn down, monks were killed or forced out of their robes, and practice went underground or disappeared. In the capital, one monastery, Gandan, was allowed to function in a limited way.
For a long time, that was nearly all.
When the communist era ended, the doors opened. Old monks who had kept their vows in secret came forward to teach.
Monasteries were rebuilt, young monks were trained, texts were printed again, and families brought children to the temples. It isn't the same as before; some things were lost for good.
But this week keeps finding the same shape: a thing broken, and people who carried it back.

how: In Mongolia, Buddhists visit monasteries such as Gandan in Ulaanbaatar to turn prayer wheels, make offerings and hear chanting, and monasteries have been rebuilt and young monks trained since the end of the communist era.

practice: Think of something that was nearly lost and came back, a language a grandparent spoke, a recipe written down just in time, a friendship mended, and picture the people who did the slow work of bringing it back.
Then let this week's others join them, nuns who rebuilt nunneries, teachers who returned, songs still sung, and rest with them.
